The core insight centers on the trade-off between signal complexity and operational reliability. The first primitive, 'Signal Decoding Complexity', encapsulates the principle that overly complex systems fail when adversaries can decode them, yet also fail when friendly forces cannot interpret them. This maps to a fundamental constraint in GSI's Bayesian inference: a signal must be robust enough for internal decoding but not so obscure as to invite misinterpretation. The second primitive, 'Tactical Execution Fidelity', captures the breakdown in communication when the quarterback ignores coach directives—this is a state transition failure in GSE where the coach's intent does not propagate to execution. The third primitive, 'System Robustness', reflects the balance between simplicity and cognitive load, where excessive complexity leads to confusion and poor performance. These primitives form a triadic structure where each interacts with the others: high complexity reduces robustness, which in turn affects fidelity. The failure mode occurs when all three converge into a singular point of breakdown—when complexity exceeds decoding capability, execution fidelity plummets, and system robustness collapses under cognitive strain.
